entities.name: Byzantine Empire under the Angelos dynasty
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Byzantine Empire under the Angelos dynasty (1185-1204 CE) governed the catastrophic final years before the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople — a 19-year period of political chaos, military incompetence, and financial exhaustion that led directly to the Latin Empire's creation and the permanent weakening of Byzantine power. The dynasty was founded by Isaac II Angelos (r. 1185-1195, 1203-1204) — a minor official who killed an imperial agent in self-defense and was proclaimed emperor by the crowd — replacing the hated Andronikos I Komnenos.

Isaac II immediately faced Bulgarian independence (1185, founding the Second Bulgarian Empire), Norman invasion of Thessalonica (1185), and constant financial crises. His brother Alexios III (r. 1195-1203) deposed and blinded him, then proved even more incompetent — famously having the Byzantine fleet's timbers sold for firewood to save money just before the Fourth Crusade arrived. The pivotal moment: Isaac's son Alexios IV fled to the West and promised the crusaders immense rewards (church unity, payment of crusade debts) to restore him to the throne.

The crusaders diverted to Constantinople (1203), restored the Angeloi, but the promised rewards never materialized; the crusaders sacked Constantinople in April 1204 — 'the most catastrophic event in Byzantine history and one of the worst atrocities of the Middle Ages.' Three days of looting, murder, and rape destroyed what had been the Christian world's richest city; Byzantine art, manuscripts, and relics were scattered across Europe. The Latin Empire (1204-1261) that replaced Byzantium was never as powerful, and when the Byzantines recaptured Constantinople (1261), the empire was permanently reduced.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Angelos dynasty — through incompetence, corruption, and the catastrophic invitation of the Fourth Crusade — caused the 1204 sack of Constantinople that permanently ended Byzantine supremacy, scattered the Christian world's greatest cultural treasures, and created the conditions for the Ottoman conquest 250 years later.
